justifications.functional_suitability: Fraud Scoring API and Case Management UI satisfy R-01 and R-02. However, R-03 (updating rules and scoring models without downtime) lacks an explicit dynamic update or deployment mechanism in the Inference Engine or API Router.
justifications.performance_efficiency: Using Go with an in-process Embedded ONNX Runtime and an asynchronous Audit Dispatcher to an AWS NLB enables low-latency scoring under 50 ms at 3,000 rps. However, Feature Assembler data sources and caching are unspecified.
justifications.compatibility: Integration with Payment Gateway / Processor Core is handled via standard gRPC and mTLS. Case Management UI integrates cleanly with external Identity Provider (IdP) over OIDC and HTTPS.
justifications.usability: The Fraud Analyst is well supported by Dashboard & Queue View and Case Detail & Explainability View. However, Risk Operations Manager / Data Scientist has no dedicated interface or tooling for managing rules and models.
justifications.reliability: The architecture omits any fallback, timeout, or fail-open mechanism to satisfy R-07 (ensuring payments are not blocked for over 1 minute if scoring becomes unavailable), creating an unmitigated single point of failure.
justifications.security: Achieves audit immutability with S3 Glacier Object Lock and pg_audit. However, explicit mechanisms for card data tokenization, field-level encryption, and masking PAN from analysts (R-05, PCI-DSS) are missing from the components.
justifications.maintainability: System decomposition into decoupled containers (Fraud Scoring API, Case Management Backend, Audit & Event Store) with clear component responsibilities supports modular maintenance by a small three-engineer team.
justifications.portability: Core logic resides in containerized Go and Node.js components suitable for AWS eu-west-1. Dependencies on proprietary services like S3 Glacier Object Lock and Aurora PostgreSQL are well-aligned with target constraints.

PERF-01.justification: Embedded ONNX runtime and an in-process Go pipeline easily achieve sub-50ms P99 at 3,000 RPS. Async audit dispatch prevents write bottlenecks. However, feature assembly data sources are not detailed.
sensitivity_points: In-process ONNX runtime eliminates network hops for ML scoring
tradeoffs: Local feature assembly avoids cache latency but limits cross-transaction state

PERF-02.justification: Scoring and case management execute in decoupled containers, keeping scoring latency isolated from analyst traffic. However, both rely on Aurora PostgreSQL without explicit read replicas for reporting queries.
sensitivity_points: Independent scaling of scoring and case management containers
tradeoffs: Shared Aurora instance between analytics and audit ingestion risks resource contention

AVAIL-01.justification: The architecture lacks a defined fallback or fail-open mechanism if Fraud Scoring API instances crash. While container orchestrators might restart tasks, no local fallback rule engine or gateway fallback path is modeled.
sensitivity_points: Absence of fail-open or fallback scoring component in the architecture
tradeoffs: Failing safe versus failing open when scoring services crash

AVAIL-02.justification: The Audit Dispatcher uses an in-memory Go channel. If Aurora or Event Ingestion Service degrades, in-memory buffers will fill, causing either dropped audit events or backpressure on scoring latency.
sensitivity_points: In-memory Go channels for audit dispatch without durable messaging
tradeoffs: Low latency via async dispatch versus durable delivery during downstream outages

MOD-01.justification: Model versioning is recorded in audit logs, but no dynamic model distribution or hot-reloading mechanism is modeled in the container. Model updates rely on external container redeployments without explicit rollback orchestration.
sensitivity_points: Hot-reloading versus rolling container deployments for ONNX models
tradeoffs: Immutable container deployments enhance stability but slow down rollback times

MOD-02.justification: The scoring API only contains an ONNX ML Inference Engine and lacks a dynamic business rules engine. Furthermore, adding velocity checks requires stateful historical lookups, which are entirely absent from the Feature Assembler.
sensitivity_points: Absence of a rule engine or velocity state store
tradeoffs: Relying purely on ONNX inference versus combining dynamic rule execution with ML

SEC-01.justification: Although authentication uses OIDC, there is no tokenization service, PAN masking component, or anomaly detection system to alert on abnormal analyst access within 15 minutes as required.
sensitivity_points: Missing tokenization/masking proxy and security monitoring integration
tradeoffs: Offloading authentication to IdP without internal behavioral anomaly detection

SEC-02.justification: The combination of capturing explanations and model versions via Audit Dispatcher, archiving to S3 Glacier with Object Lock, and 7-year WORM retention directly and completely satisfies the regulatory retrieval requirement.
sensitivity_points: Immutable WORM compliance via S3 Glacier Object Lock for 7 years
tradeoffs: Archival retrieval latency from Glacier versus long-term storage costs
